people.desc: Kim Do-yoon is a second-year PhD student in chemical engineering at Yonsei. He plays keyboard for the young adults' worship team at a large Presbyterian church in Gangnam, and he still goes to 5 a.m. dawn prayer a couple of times a week, mostly because his mother does. He finished his army service at 23. He is quiet, conscientious and anxious about publications, and he is privately embarrassed by pastors who turn up at political rallies. His grandmother, whom he adores, is a lifelong Buddhist and has never let him pray for her out loud.

notes.note: Dawn prayer happens in a full sanctuary, yet it is his most private time with God. He wanted a 'both' option and settled on Not sure.
He thought of Rahab and the Hebrew midwives and could not decide whether they were praised for the lie or for their faith. Not sure.
Slightly confusing: 'a good person' could mean ordinary decency or being right with God. He answered as if it meant the second, which is why it came out Strongly disagree.
Filial duty weighs heavily on him. He chose his own field against his father, so he agreed, but the word 'begs' made him hesitate.
He believes church discipline is biblical, but he has seen it used on people who fell out with an elder. 'Put out' sounded harsh, so he tapped Not sure.
The doctrine he was taught says no, but his grandmother came to mind at once. He tapped Disagree slowly.

people.overall: It felt gentle and quick, and less churchy than he expected. A few items made him stop longer than he wanted to on a quiz, especially the ones that brought his grandmother and Rahab to mind.

people.seed: Brazilian Catholic grandmother in the charismatic renewal, 68, Sao Paulo
people.desc: Dona Aparecida Souza is a widowed former school cook in Itaquera, on the east side of Sao Paulo. For twenty years she has led a Tuesday night Renovacao Carismatica prayer group at her parish. She prays in tongues, says the rosary on the bus, never misses the healing Mass on Cancao Nova, and cooks for any neighbour who is short that week. She laughs loudly, cries easily and talks without stopping. Her youngest son lives with his boyfriend in Rio. She loves him fiercely and visits twice a year, but she does not bring it up at church.

notes.note: She agreed because of the proverb that flies can't get into a closed mouth, laughing because she never manages it herself.
She knows the Church says not to lie, but her heart says a mother lies to protect her child. She tapped Agree and felt a little guilty.
Confusing to her. The stories happened AND they mean something, so she didn't see why she had to choose. Not sure.
She would say it takes God's grace and you have to do your part. Disagree was the nearest answer.
She has never thought about a 'just war'. She only knows she hates war, so she disagreed.
'Only God knows.' She prays for the souls in purgatory and hopes for mercy for everyone, but she believes hell is real. Not sure.

people.overall: She enjoyed it and wanted to talk about every question with someone. A couple of sentences sounded like a university and not like her life, especially the heart that is never stirred and the Bible stories' 'deeper meaning'.

people.seed: Ex-evangelical in the middle of "deconstructing", 31, Denver
people.desc: Jordan Mercer grew up in a Colorado Springs megachurch, led his youth group's purity pledge at 15, and graduated from a small Christian college in Idaho. He is now a UX designer in Denver. He is in therapy, listens to deconstruction podcasts on the drive to the fourteeners he climbs, and honestly doesn't know whether he believes in God, though he still prays when he is scared on a ridge. He is funny, sarcastic, quick to feel manipulated, and angry about how his old church handled a youth pastor's abuse case. He still loves the Psalms and the Jesus of the Gospels, and he gets defensive when atheist friends mock either.

notes.note: 'Grow closer to God' assumes there is someone to get close to. He answered as the version of himself that still prays on ridges, where it feels more real than church ever did.
Loaded for him: 'it's your job' is how his church's accountability groups talked. He would speak up about real harm, but not about someone's sex life or drinking.
He can't answer as a believer, so Not sure was also true. He picked Disagree because 'God told me in a dream' was used at his church to shut down any discussion.
Loaded for him. He loves mystery, but 'better left alone' reads like 'stop asking questions', which is what his youth pastor said. He disagreed with the phrasing as much as the idea.
His instinct is that 'God is calling me' is often ego or cult talk, but he respects people who left their families for good reasons.
He rejects the 'you're a worm who can do nothing' teaching he grew up with, but therapy taught him how much depends on the people around you. Agree was the nearest answer.
'If there is a God, yes.' He hopes it more than he believes it.

people.overall: Surprisingly not triggering, and a few items felt like they came from someone who got it. He watched for a trap on every screen, and two or three wordings ('your job', 'better left alone') sounded like his old church.

people.seed: Convert to Christianity from a Muslim family who cut him off, 36, Toronto
people.desc: Imran Qureshi is a hospital pharmacist who grew up in a devout Pakistani Sunni family in Mississauga. He was baptised at 29, after two years of secretly reading a Gospel of John that a coworker gave him, and after a dream he still cannot describe without his voice catching. When his father found out, the family cut him off. His mother still sends him one text every Eid. He goes to a multi-ethnic Anglican church downtown, fasts twice a week from a habit he refuses to break, and reads Scripture with the seriousness he once gave the Qur'an. He is disciplined and careful with words, and a little impatient with Canadian Christians who treat faith as a hobby.

notes.note: He met Christ alone, reading at night, but the church became the only family he has. He was genuinely torn and tapped Not sure.
He hid his baptism for two years and once lied to protect another secret believer. He thinks it was right and is still uneasy about it.

His family demanded to know how God could have a Son, and he had to find answers. He dislikes leaving questions alone, though he admits some of what is said about the Trinity can't be fully explained.
His head says a church should hold a standard. But he knows what it is to be put out of a community, and that decided it: Disagree.
He believes a person must come to Christ. His mother came to mind at once, and he tapped Disagree with difficulty.

people.overall: It felt serious and fair, and nothing gave away what it was after. The questions about calling, protective lies and whether God saves everyone were personal enough that he'd want to know who wrote them.

people.seed: Non-religious software founder who loves Stoic philosophy, 40, Austin
people.desc: Derek Lindqvist was confirmed Lutheran in suburban Minnesota at 14 and never went back. He sold his first logistics-software company and now runs his second in Austin. He reads a page of Marcus Aurelius every morning, journals and runs ultramarathons, and he calls himself 'not religious, not anti-religious'. He co-parents a nine-year-old daughter with his ex-wife and gives quietly to a local food bank. When his father died last year he sobbed at the funeral in front of half his sales team, which embarrassed him and has left him less sure about Stoic calm than he used to be.

notes.note: 'Your faith' doesn't apply to him, since he has none. He agreed with the spirit of it.
He doesn't believe in God, so there is nothing to grow closer to. Not sure was the least wrong answer.
The 'see them again' part doesn't apply to him. He answered the second half, remembering his father's funeral.
He agreed only if 'God' means the order of nature, the Stoic logos, and not the Christian God.
This is textbook Stoicism, but since his father's funeral he no longer thinks being unmoved is the ideal. Agree, not Strongly agree.
He agreed, but because questions about God aren't worth his time, not out of reverence.
He read 'God is calling you' as 'a deep conviction about your life's work'. He did that himself when he dropped out against his parents' wishes to start a company.
He answered as if the church were any organisation with values: you let go of people who won't live by the culture.
He isn't a Christian, so he answered for the Christians he knows.
In his view there is no God to save anyone. Disagree would suggest a God who chooses not to save some, so he tapped Not sure.

people.overall: Easy and pleasant, and it didn't feel like it was trying to convert him. About a third of the items assume a believer, so he spent the quiz translating 'God' into something he could answer.
